questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Ecology: The Three Properties That Define a Population
questions.learningObjective: name the three properties that describe a population rather than a set of individuals
questions.stem: Ecologists treat a population as a distinct unit of study rather than a collection of separate organisms. Which three properties together define it?

options.text: Its size, its density in the area occupied, and the pattern of spacing of its individuals
Its size, the age of its oldest member, and the number of species present with it
options.misconception: believes a population can include several species and is defined by a record length

options.text: Its density, its average body size, and the total mass of the individuals in it
options.misconception: describes properties of the individuals rather than of the group they form

options.text: Its size, its colour, and the number of separate groups the individuals form
options.misconception: takes a visible trait and a group count as defining properties of a population

questions.explanation: A population is the members of one species within a defined area, and it is described by three properties: how many individuals it has, how many of those are packed into the area it occupies, and how they are spaced relative to one another. The spacing matters because the same size and density can be arranged evenly, randomly or in clumps, and those three arrangements expose the population to different conditions, so the pattern is a property in its own right. The tempting belief that the number of species belongs to a population fails because a population holds one species, and several populations in one place make a community. The belief about body size and total mass fails because those describe individuals rather than the group, and the belief about colour fails because a uniform-looking set of individuals can still be one clumped population.
questions.hint: Ask what can be measured about a group that says nothing about any single member.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Ecology: What Separates a Community from an Ecosystem
questions.learningObjective: distinguish a community from an ecosystem by what each term includes
questions.stem: Two terms are used for a stretch of woodland, and one of them is meant to include the non-living surroundings. Which pairing is correct?

options.text: A community is the populations present; an ecosystem adds the non-living parts and their exchanges
A community is one species; an ecosystem is the set of every species sharing that habitat
options.misconception: confuses a population with a community and puts species in the wrong term

options.text: A community includes the soil and light; an ecosystem is limited to the trees and other plants
options.misconception: puts the physical surroundings in the community and leaves them out of the ecosystem

options.text: A community is a single hectare; an ecosystem is the whole planet regardless of its living parts
options.misconception: defines the terms by area rather than by what each one includes

questions.explanation: A community is the set of populations of different species living and interacting in one place, so it is entirely a living description. An ecosystem is that community plus the non-living components of the same place, the light, water, soil and temperature, together with the exchanges of energy and nutrients between them. The two words differ by what they leave out, not by their size. The tempting belief that a community is one species fails because one species in one place is a population. The belief that an ecosystem is only the plants fails because it must include the animals, the decomposers and the physical conditions. The belief that a community is an area fails because a community can be defined at whatever scale is convenient, and the belief about the planet fails because the scale of an ecosystem is set by the processes being studied rather than by the whole world.
questions.hint: Ask what each term adds that the other does not.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Ecology: Separating a Habitat from a Niche
questions.learningObjective: distinguish where an organism lives from what it does there
questions.stem: Two species may be found in the same woodland yet keep completely out of each other's way. Which pair of statements separates the place an organism occupies from the role it plays?

options.text: The habitat is the place, while the niche is the range of conditions used and the resources taken
The habitat is the role, while the niche is the place where that role is carried out
options.misconception: swaps the two terms so the place and the role are attached wrongly

options.text: The habitat is the set of resources used, while the niche is the area in which they are found
options.misconception: swaps resources and area, giving the place the role and the role the place

options.text: The habitat is the whole ecosystem, while the niche is one particular population within it
options.misconception: uses ecosystem and population instead of habitat and niche

questions.explanation: The habitat answers where the organism lives, and it is a place that can be shared by many species at once. The niche answers how it lives: which part of the food it takes, the range of temperature and moisture it tolerates, when it is active, and which other species it meets there. Two species can therefore share a habitat and still occupy different niches, which is the usual reason they can both persist in the same place. The tempting belief that the terms are reversed fails because a role cannot be a location. The belief that resources and area are the two terms fails because that is the niche against the habitat stated the other way round. The belief that the habitat means the whole ecosystem fails because a habitat may be a single pond within it.
questions.hint: Ask which term would still make sense if the organism were moved somewhere else.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Ecology: What Species Richness Cannot Tell You
questions.learningObjective: explain why two communities with the same richness can differ in diversity
questions.stem: Two ponds hold three species each. In one the individuals are spread fairly evenly between the species, and in the other one species accounts for most of the animals. What does the count of species fail to reveal about the second pond?

options.text: That its diversity is lower, because a few species hold nearly all of the individuals
That its diversity is higher, because more individuals of a dominant species raise the total
options.misconception: believes a longer head count raises diversity when the species count has not changed

options.text: That its richness is higher as well, because the dominant species is counted repeatedly
options.misconception: believes repeated counts of one species add species to the tally

options.text: That its diversity matches the first pond, because richness and diversity are one measure
options.misconception: treats richness and diversity as the same number rather than as two

questions.explanation: Richness counts species and nothing else, so two ponds with the same number of species tie on that measure even when one of them is close to being a single-species pond. Diversity adds the distribution of individuals, so a community in which one species holds most of the individuals scores lower than an evenly matched one, and that is the information richness throws away. The tempting belief that a dominant species raises diversity fails because every extra individual of the same species adds nothing to the count of species and a great deal to the imbalance. The belief that richness is also higher fails because counting a species twice is not counting a new one. The belief that the two terms are one measure fails because the whole reason for using a diversity index is to correct the blind spot that richness has.
questions.hint: Ask what a count of species ignores about the individuals it counted.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Ecology: What Constant Per-Capita Rate Means in a Growth Phase
questions.learningObjective: distinguish a constant per-capita growth rate from a constant absolute rate
questions.stem: A population in its rapid growth phase doubles at the same rate whether it holds a hundred individuals or a hundred thousand. What is constant during that phase?

options.text: The rate per individual, so the total added each step still rises as the population grows
The total number of individuals added at each step, so the population rises by a fixed amount
options.misconception: believes a fixed head count is added each step, which would give a straight line

options.text: The birth rate alone, while the death rate rises to keep the per-capita rate constant
options.misconception: makes the per-capita rate constant by moving the deaths rather than the fraction

options.text: The number of individuals alive, since a doubling phase leaves the count unchanged by definition
options.misconception: believes a phase named for doubling somehow leaves the population the same size

questions.explanation: The rapid phase is exponential, and the defining feature is that a fixed fraction of the population is added in each unit of time rather than a fixed number, so the per-capita rate is constant while the absolute rate climbs with the population. That is why the curve has no straight sections and why a phase is often named the logarithmic one. The tempting belief that a fixed number is added at each step fails because that would produce a straight line rather than a steepening one, and no population could keep doubling in that way for long. The belief that births alone are constant fails because a constant fraction of a rising population means rising births. The belief that the count is unchanged fails because doubling changes it by definition.
questions.hint: Decide whether the same number or the same fraction is being added each step.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Ecology: What Sets the Level a Population Stabilises At
questions.learningObjective: explain why the level a population stabilises at depends on the resource and the environment
questions.stem: Two populations of the same species are given different amounts of the same food in otherwise identical conditions, and they stabilise at different sizes. What does the different final size show?

options.text: The level a population settles at is set by the resource and the environment, not by the species alone
The level a population settles at is a fixed property of the species that the environment cannot move
options.misconception: believes a final level belongs to the species and cannot be moved by the conditions

options.text: The level a population settles at is set by the birth rate alone, since the death rate follows from it
options.misconception: leaves the losses out of the balance that fixes the final level

options.text: The level a population settles at is set by how large the founding group happened to be
options.misconception: believes the starting head count fixes where the population ends up

questions.explanation: The level a population stabilises at is where the constraints of the situation stop it growing: the resource that runs short first, the space, the rate at which waste is removed. Change the resource and the level moves, which is why the same species can reach different numbers in different places, and why adding a resource or improving conditions can raise the level rather than merely letting the population get there faster. The tempting belief that it is a fixed property of the species fails because the two populations here are the same species at different levels. The belief that births alone set it fails because a rising birth rate with a matching rise in deaths still gives no net growth. The belief that the founding group sets it fails because a small start can grow to the same level as a large one given the same resources.
questions.hint: Ask what the two populations share and what the experiment actually varied.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Ecology: The Test That Separates the Two Kinds of Limit
questions.learningObjective: state the test that distinguishes a density-dependent from a density-independent factor
questions.stem: Ecologists sort the factors that hold a population down into two kinds. What does an observer have to measure in order to place a factor in the right group?

options.text: Whether the effect of the factor gets stronger as the population gets more crowded
Whether the factor is a living thing or a non-living part of the surroundings
options.misconception: uses the living and non-living split, which cuts across both groups

options.text: Whether the factor acts on the young individuals or only on the adults
options.misconception: bases the classification on the age of the individuals affected instead of on crowding

options.text: Whether the factor was present in the past year or arrived only recently
options.misconception: bases the classification on when the factor arrived rather than on its effect

questions.explanation: The distinguishing measurement is how the strength of the effect changes with crowding, and that is the whole content of the two names. Competition, disease and predation act harder as the individuals meet more often, so they are density-dependent, while a frost, a flood or a sudden change in temperature hit the same way whatever the crowding and are density-independent. The tempting belief that the living and non-living split is the test fails because disease is living and crowding-dependent, while a drought is non-living and crowding-independent, so the split cuts across both groups. The belief about age fails because a factor can act on either. The belief about timing fails because a factor that has always been present can still be density-dependent.
questions.hint: Ask what would have to be varied for the factor's effect to change.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Ecology: The Two Shapes of a Growth Curve
questions.learningObjective: distinguish the unbounded and the decelerating growth models by their shape
questions.stem: Two growth models are used for a population, and one of them assumes the constraints of the real world never bite. Which pair of statements separates them?

options.text: The unbounded model curves upwards for ever, the other rises and then levels off as limits bite
The unbounded model levels off as limits bite, the other curves upwards for ever instead
options.misconception: reverses the two shapes so the ceiling is attached to the wrong model

options.text: Both curve upwards for ever, and the difference between them is only the size of the start
options.misconception: denies that the two models differ in shape at all

options.text: Both level off, and the difference between them is only how long the rising part lasts
options.misconception: denies that one model has a ceiling and the other has none

questions.explanation: The unbounded model assumes each individual produces more than it replaces, so a constant fraction of a rising population is added at every step and the curve steepens without any ceiling. The other model includes the idea that limits tighten as the population grows, so the per-capita rate falls as the population approaches the level the environment can support, and the curve flattens there. The first is a useful short-term description and a bad long-term one. The tempting belief that the terms are reversed fails because a model with no ceiling cannot level off and one with a ceiling cannot keep steepening. The belief that the starting size is the only difference fails because the starting size does not change the shape at all. The belief that the models are the same shape fails because the ceiling is the entire content of the second.
questions.hint: Ask which of the two models has a ceiling, and what produces it.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Ecology: What a Trophic Level Counts
questions.learningObjective: define a trophic level by the number of transfer steps from a producer
questions.stem: A food web is described in terms of trophic levels rather than of named species. What does a member's trophic level count?

options.text: The number of transfer steps between it and the primary producers that start the chain
The number of species it eats, however small or unrelated each of those species is
options.misconception: counts the kinds of prey rather than the steps back to the producers

options.text: The number of times the energy passing through it has been used before it arrives
options.misconception: counts energy uses, which is the same at every level and so says nothing about position

options.text: The number of feeding steps in the whole web, whether or not it takes part in them
options.misconception: counts the whole web rather than the part of it the organism occupies

questions.explanation: A trophic level records position in the transfer chain, and it is found by counting steps away from the producers: the producers are the first level, the organisms eating them the second, and so on. That is why a species eating at two places sits at more than one level at once, and why a web is usually drawn with links that cross levels rather than a tidy ladder. The tempting belief that it counts the species eaten fails because the count of species is not the count of steps, and a single predator can eat across several levels. The belief that it counts energy uses fails because the number of uses at a level is the same for everyone on it, so it says nothing about position. The belief that it counts the whole web fails because the web is shared and a level is a local property.
questions.hint: Start from the producers and ask how many steps away the organism sits.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Ecology: Why So Little Energy Passes Between Levels
questions.learningObjective: explain why transfer between trophic levels is inefficient
questions.stem: Only a small fraction of the energy in one level becomes new tissue at the next. What accounts for where the rest goes?

options.text: Most is spent on respiration, movement and repair, and leaves as heat that nothing can reassemble
Most is lost because the animals fail to digest their food before excreting what is left
options.misconception: makes undigested material the main loss rather than a secondary one

options.text: Most is lost because the next level is too small to take up the supply that is available
options.misconception: blames the size of the next level instead of the running cost of the current one

options.text: Most is lost because energy cannot be stored in tissue without a supply of oxygen to burn it
options.misconception: turns a condition for respiration into the route by which energy is lost

questions.explanation: Every level spends a large share of what it takes in simply running itself: breathing, moving, maintaining temperature, replacing worn cells and digesting food. That work ends as heat, and heat at body temperature cannot be gathered up by another organism to do work, so the energy is genuinely lost from the chain rather than merely moved along it. The remainder is stored as new tissue and is what the next level can take. The tempting belief that digestion is the main loss fails because digestion does account for part of it, but the larger share is the running cost of staying alive, and undigested material is not energy lost so much as material never taken up. The belief that the next level is too small fails because a smaller level can still capture what is available. The belief about oxygen fails because it describes a condition for respiration rather than a route of loss.
questions.hint: Ask what an animal has to spend energy on merely to stay alive.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Ecology: The Three Ways Organisms Get Their Energy
questions.learningObjective: separate producers, consumers and decomposers by the source of their energy
questions.stem: Organisms in an ecosystem are sorted into three groups by where their energy comes from. Which grouping is correct?

options.text: Producers build tissue from sunlight, consumers from other organisms, decomposers from remains
Producers eat other organisms, consumers make their own food, decomposers do neither
options.misconception: reverses the roles of producers and consumers and empties the decomposers

options.text: Producers and consumers both make their own food, and decomposers eat only living prey
options.misconception: gives consumers the producer's job and the decomposers a living rather than a dead supply

options.text: Producers eat sunlight, consumers eat plants only, and decomposers eat animals only
options.misconception: treats sunlight as food and ties each group to one kingdom instead of one carbon source

questions.explanation: The three groups are separated by the source of the carbon in their tissue. Producers take carbon out of the non-living environment, chiefly carbon dioxide, and build tissue with energy from sunlight. Consumers get their carbon from tissue that another organism has already built, whether living or dead. Decomposers are consumers of a special kind, taking carbon from dead remains and waste, which is what returns the nutrients to the environment for producers to use again. The tempting belief that producers eat fails because they make rather than take in organic material. The belief that consumers make their own food fails because no animal does. The belief that decomposers eat only live prey fails because they cannot and their role depends on what has already died. The belief that consumers and decomposers are tied to particular kingdoms fails because both take in carbon that has already been built into tissue.
questions.hint: Ask where the carbon in each group's tissue was before the organism took it in.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Ecology: A Nutrient Cycle and Its Reservoir
questions.learningObjective: identify a cycle's reservoir and explain why one nutrient differs from the others
questions.stem: Carbon and nitrogen both spend a large part of their cycle in the air, while phosphorus does not. What follows from that difference for phosphorus?

options.text: Its cycle runs mainly through rock and soil, so it moves over long distances far more slowly
Its cycle runs mainly through rock and soil, so it moves over long distances far more quickly
options.misconception: keeps the right reservoir and reverses the speed the reservoir implies

options.text: Its cycle is unaffected by living things because no organism takes it into its tissue at all
options.misconception: denies that phosphorus passes through living tissue at all

options.text: Its cycle is faster than the others because the same phosphorus is reused many times each year
options.misconception: compounds the reuse idea into a claim of a faster cycle overall

questions.explanation: A reservoir is the large store a nutrient sits in between its passages through living things, and it sets the pace of the whole cycle. Carbon's largest reservoir is the atmosphere and carbon in rock, and nitrogen's is the air, so both are moved over great distances by wind and water. Phosphorus has no comparable gaseous store, so its reservoir is rock and soil, and the phosphorus available to plants has to reach them by weathering of rock or by the slow breakdown of organic material in the soil. The result is a cycle that is local and slow, and that is why a region's phosphorus supply is so tightly tied to its own geology while its carbon supply is not. The tempting belief that it moves quickly fails because there is no air to carry it anywhere. The belief that no organism uses it fails because every organism takes phosphorus into its tissue. The belief that faster reuse compensates fails because reuse still runs through the same slow local reservoirs.
questions.hint: Ask how the phosphorus would have to travel from one place to another with no air to carry it.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Ecology: Why an Organism Makes a Substance Other Organisms Cannot Use
questions.learningObjective: explain why a producer of an antibiotic gains by making one
questions.stem: A fungus produces a substance that stops competing bacteria from growing, and people grow the fungus to obtain the substance. Why is making it a good strategy for the fungus rather than a pointless one?

options.text: It suppresses the bacteria that would otherwise take the same food, and it does so near where they are
It supplies the fungus with a nutrient it cannot build for itself out of what it has
options.misconception: treats the substance as a nutrient rather than as a way of removing rivals

options.text: It lets the fungus use the bacteria as a food source once they have stopped growing
options.misconception: turns an inhibitor into a meal and misses that growth is stopped

options.text: It discourages the animals that would otherwise eat the fungus, by making them ill
options.misconception: redirects the effect from bacterial competitors to herbivores

questions.explanation: A substance that suppresses the growth of competing bacteria is a way of holding ground against organisms that would take the same food and the same space, and it is a secondary product rather than a part of the fungus's own machinery, which is why it is usually only made in large amounts when the fungus is competing for that food. Making it close to where the competitors are is what makes it work, because the effect is local rather than a general one. The tempting belief that it is a nutrient fails because the substance is used by others to stop growth rather than to build anything. The belief that it turns the bacteria into food fails because they are inhibited, not encouraged. The belief that it deters animals fails because the substance targets bacterial growth, and defending against herbivores is a separate line of defence.
questions.hint: Ask who the substance actually harms, and what they would otherwise have taken.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Ecology: Classifying a Pair of Species by Their Effects
questions.learningObjective: classify an interaction by the sign of the effect on each of the two species
questions.stem: Three kinds of close association between two species are named, and they are distinguished by what happens to each partner. On what basis are the three told apart?

options.text: By the sign of the effect on each partner, giving one, two or no beneficiaries in the pair
By how long the association lasts, separating the brief from the permanent arrangements
options.misconception: sorts the three by duration rather than by the effect on each partner

options.text: By how close the two are physically, separating contact from separation over a distance
options.misconception: sorts the three by physical contact rather than by the effect on each partner

options.text: By how many individuals take part, separating pairs from whole mixed communities
options.misconception: sorts the three by group size rather than by the effect on each partner

questions.explanation: The classification turns on two signs: what happens to each of the two species. One benefits and the other is harmed, which is the arrangement a parasite and its host make. One benefits and the other is unaffected, which is what a relationship benefiting a pollinator or a seed spreader looks like from the plant's side. Both benefit, which is the arrangement in which two species do better together than apart. The names describe the effect, not the intimacy, the duration or the number involved. The tempting belief that duration is the test fails because a long association can be any of the three kinds. The belief about physical closeness fails because a relationship can be maintained over a long distance. The belief about the number of individuals involved fails because all three kinds occur between a single pair.
questions.hint: Ask what happens to each partner, separately, and then name the arrangement.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Ecology: What Competitive Exclusion Requires
questions.learningObjective: state the conditions under which competitive exclusion must follow
questions.stem: Two species that grow perfectly well on their own fail to coexist when they are grown together on one limiting resource. Under which set of conditions is that outcome forced rather than likely?

options.text: The same single resource limits both, they occupy the same place, and no refuge interrupts the contest
The resource is unlimited, they occupy the same place, and growth is identical in both
options.misconception: supplies a reason for both to persist and so removes the contest

options.text: The two occupy different parts of the same habitat, and the resource is renewed slowly
options.misconception: removes the overlap that exclusion depends on rather than supplying it

options.text: One species has a higher birth rate, the two use different food, and the area is very large
options.misconception: gives them different food and so denies the shared limiting resource

questions.explanation: Exclusion follows when the two are competing for exactly the same thing in exactly the same place, because whichever gets the resource first leaves less for the other, and the one that is slightly better at capturing it ends up with all of it while the other fails. The result is a contest with no draws. The tempting belief that an unlimited resource produces exclusion fails because nothing is scarce, so there is nothing to contest. The belief that occupying different parts allows exclusion fails because using different fractions of the resource is precisely what removes the contest. The belief about a higher birth rate and different food fails because different food means they are not competing for the same thing, so the higher birth rate cannot drive the other out by that mechanism.
questions.hint: Ask whether the two are taking the same thing from the same place.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Ecology: How Two Species Avoid the Same Contest
questions.learningObjective: explain how using different parts of a resource lets two species persist together
questions.stem: Two species that would exclude one another if they took the same resource manage to persist side by side. What change in how they use the resource makes that possible?

options.text: Each takes a different part of it, so neither depends on the part the other depends on
Each takes the same part of it but a smaller share, leaving more for the other one
options.misconception: keeps both on the same pool and expects a share to solve the problem

options.text: Each takes the same part of it but only when the other is absent from the place
options.misconception: makes them take turns on one pool rather than using different parts of it

options.text: Each takes a different part of it, so together they exhaust what each one alone would use
options.misconception: pairs the right mechanism with the outcome that ends coexistence

questions.explanation: Two species persist together when what each depends on is not what the other depends on, so the competition that would have ended in exclusion simply does not arise. The two may take the same kind of food but at different heights in the canopy, or from different depths of soil, or at different times of day, and in each case the overlap is removed without either giving up its resource entirely. The same account applies to predators sharing prey but hunting in different places or times. The tempting belief that smaller shares solve it fails because both still depend on the same pool, and a shortfall hits both. The belief that taking turns solves it fails because alternating still leaves each unable to reach the level it would reach alone. The belief about exhausting the resource fails because that describes what stops them persisting.
questions.hint: Ask whether each species still depends on the same pool of resource after the change.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Ecology: What Predation Does to a Prey Population's Level
questions.learningObjective: state the effect of a predator on the level a prey population settles at
questions.stem: A prey population is doing well on its own and settles at a high level, and the same prey settles lower once a predator is present. What does the predator change, and what does that change do to the prey?

options.text: It lowers the level the prey settles at, because prey is now removed as well as born
It raises the level the prey settles at, because the predator limits the prey it competes with
options.misconception: borrows the indirect effect a predator has on a competitor for the direct one

options.text: It leaves the level unchanged, because births rise to replace every individual taken
options.misconception: assumes the losses are made good exactly, which would leave nothing to observe

options.text: It lowers the level the prey settles at, because the prey then eats more and so grows faster
options.misconception: keeps the right direction and invents a faster growth that would defeat it

questions.explanation: Adding a predator introduces a second loss term to the prey's balance, so the point at which births stop covering losses moves down and the average size of the prey population is lower than it was alone. In a system where the prey is also limited by its own food, the total losses now include being eaten as well as running short, and the population settles where the two together balance the births. The tempting belief that a predator raises the prey level fails because that is the whole result of a predator suppressing a competitor or a more efficient forager, not the direct effect. The belief that births fully replace the losses fails because then nothing would be happening. The belief about the prey eating more fails because a lower prey density means less food per individual, which works against them.
questions.hint: Add a second loss to the prey's balance and see where the two now balance the births.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Ecology: What Makes a Species Keystone Rather Than Merely Numerous
questions.learningObjective: state what a keystone species is defined by relative to its abundance
questions.stem: Some rarely seen species hold an entire community together, while abundant species can be removed with little visible change. What does the term keystone single out?

options.text: A large effect per individual, so the influence is out of all proportion to how few there are
A large effect in total, so the influence follows from how numerous the species is
options.misconception: defines the group by total effect and so makes it the opposite of a keystone

options.text: A large effect on one other species only, with the rest of the community left untouched
options.misconception: restricts the effect to a single partner and drops the community-wide change

options.text: A large effect at one point in time only, which disappears once conditions change again
options.misconception: makes the effect temporary, which contradicts a structural role in the community

questions.explanation: The term marks a species whose effect on the rest of the community is large in proportion to how few of it there are, which is a statement about effect per individual rather than about total effect. That is why the test of a keystone species is what happens when it is removed: if the community changes far more than its numbers would suggest, it qualifies. It also explains why the group is defined by a relationship rather than by a list, because the same species can be keystone in one place and unimportant in another where its food or its predators are absent. The tempting belief that keystone means numerous fails because the two are opposites. The belief that only one other species is affected fails because the defining feature is a spread through the community. The belief that the effect is temporary fails because an effect that reverses is not a structural role.

questions.topic: Ecology: The Two Things That Make an Introduced Species Damaging
questions.learningObjective: state the two features that let an introduced species damage an established community

They eat more than their own weight, and they are larger than the species already present
options.misconception: picks appetite and size, neither of which explains a spread through a community

options.misconception: pairs a condition that prevents establishment with one that releases them

questions.learningObjective: explain why succession on bare ground begins with organisms that build soil

There is too much light on bare ground, so the first job is to shade the surface below it
options.misconception: turns a job done by the later canopy into the first obstacle on bare ground

options.text: There are no animals present to spread seeds, so the first job is to supply the grazers
options.misconception: makes the grazers a prerequisite for the first soil rather than a later arrival

options.text: There is no dead material to break down, so the first job is to supply the decomposers
options.misconception: moves the source of the first organic material to somewhere it already is

questions.topic: Ecology: The Assumption That Undermines the Term Climax
questions.learningObjective: explain why the idea of a fixed climax community is contested
questions.stem: An old account of succession says each community passes through stages until it reaches a final one that stays put. What assumption underneath that account has been undermined?

options.text: That a final stable composition exists at all, since communities keep changing after they appear settled
That communities can be sorted into stages at all, since no two sites follow the same order
options.misconception: attacks the staging rather than the existence of an endpoint

options.text: That the first colonisers matter, since soil on bare ground is usually already present
options.misconception: describes secondary succession and takes it for the case the term covers

options.text: That disturbance occurs, since a site without disturbance would reach its final state sooner
options.misconception: treats a missing disturbance as the problem, though it was always in the account

Long records of communities show that they do not settle, that species keep arriving and leaving, and that the composition keeps shifting, so a climax is at best a description of a long plateau rather than a fixed state. That is why the term is now often used cautiously and paired with a word like potential. The tempting belief that staging is the problem fails because repeated studies do find broadly similar orders, and the order is not what is in doubt. The belief that soil is usually already present fails because that describes secondary succession, which is not the case the terminus was proposed for. The belief that disturbance is the problem fails because disturbance was always part of the old account, and a site without it would not stay fixed either.

questions.topic: Ecology: The Steps of Speciation by Geographic Isolation
questions.learningObjective: sequence the mechanism by which a barrier can produce a new species
questions.stem: Speciation by geographic isolation proceeds through several stages rather than in one step. Which sequence describes it correctly?

options.text: A barrier separates the groups, they diverge, they meet again, and only then are they fully separate
A barrier separates the groups, they meet again at once, and divergence follows from the meeting
options.misconception: puts the two groups back in contact before there is anything to diverge

options.text: The groups diverge first, a barrier appears later, and being together then makes them species
options.misconception: reverses cause and effect by needing the barrier to come after the divergence

options.text: A barrier separates the groups, they diverge, and the barrier makes them species without any meeting
options.misconception: lets a geographic accident stand in for the biological test of separation

questions.explanation: A barrier in the landscape stops the flow of individuals between groups, and the two then diverge on their own as mutation, chance loss and different selection each push the allele frequencies apart. Divergence alone is not yet speciation, because the two could still interbreed if the barrier were lifted. Speciation is complete when reproductive isolation has built up, and that can be revealed when the two meet again and the offspring are inviable, sterile or simply not produced, or when behaviour has changed so much they do not try. The tempting belief that meeting comes before divergence fails because there is nothing to meet with while the barrier holds, and a population cannot diverge by exchanging members. The belief that divergence comes first fails because divergence in one continuously connected group is held in check by the exchange of individuals. The belief that the barrier alone finishes the job fails because a barrier is a geographic accident, not a biological property.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Ecology: What Chance Does to a Small Population
questions.learningObjective: explain why chance changes allele frequencies more in a small population
questions.stem: A few individuals are the only survivors of a population, and the allele frequencies in the survivors turn out to be different from those before. What explains the change, and what would not have happened in a large population?

options.text: The survivors happened to carry different proportions of the alleles by chance, and this is a bottleneck
The survivors adapted to the new conditions, and this is a case of natural selection acting at once
options.misconception: replaces a change in proportions with a claim that the forms themselves improved

options.text: The alleles in the survivors were stronger, and they outcompeted the forms they replaced
options.misconception: credits the alleles with a new property that the survivors did not acquire

options.text: The two allele forms merged into one, and the survivors simply had fewer of them to carry
options.misconception: assumes two alleles at one locus fused into a single form

questions.explanation: A small group carries only a sample of the alleles the whole population held, and which alleles it happens to carry is down to luck, so its frequencies differ from the original by chance alone. A sharp reduction of this kind is a bottleneck, and the companion case is a founder group, a handful that starts a population somewhere new. Both produce the same kind of change, and the reason a large population escapes it is scale: in a large group the sampling error is a small fraction of the total, whereas in a small group the same proportion of error is most of the sample. The tempting belief that this is adaptation fails because no trait improved, only the proportions of what was already there changed. The belief that the alleles were stronger fails because nothing about the alleles themselves changed. The belief that forms merged fails because two alleles at one locus do not fuse into one another.
questions.hint: Ask whether anything about the alleles themselves changed, or only how many of each there were.

questions.topic: Ecology: The Condition Most Often Missing From a Selection Claim
questions.learningObjective: identify the requirement that a trait's frequency changes across generations for selection
questions.stem: For a trait to be described as having been selected, three things must all be true of it. Which of them is the one a single round of observation is most likely to miss?

options.text: That the trait's frequency in the population changes over successive generations of the trait
That the trait is present in every individual of the population at the time it is measured
options.misconception: requires a trait to be universal, which leaves nothing for selection to sort on

options.text: That the trait is passed to offspring, so that it can be inherited rather than re-formed
options.misconception: picks inheritance, which is the requirement most easily demonstrated

options.text: That the trait shows a measurable difference between individuals in the same generation
options.misconception: picks variation, which is normally the first thing measured

A single generation can show the first two and still show nothing about the third, because the effect on survival and breeding has to be converted into a shift in the numbers of individuals carrying the trait, and that is a statement about several generations rather than one. This is the requirement that makes selection different from an accident in one round. The tempting belief that the trait must be in every individual fails because the point of selection is that it is not, and a trait that everybody has cannot be sorted on. The belief that inheritance alone is what is missed fails because inheritance is usually easy to demonstrate. The belief that variation is what is missed fails because variation is usually the first thing measured.

questions.topic: Ecology: Reading Gains and Per-Capita Rates Together
questions.learningObjective: read a count series and tell a rising total gain from a falling per-capita rate

stimulus.body: Survey note (written for this course): An open population of one species is counted every year for ten years and the counts are 500, 640, 790, 950, 1,110, 1,250, 1,360, 1,440, 1,490, 1,520 and 1,536. The gains between successive counts are therefore 140, 150, 160, 160, 140, 110, 80, 50, 30 and 16 individuals. Dividing each count by the one before it gives 1.28, 1.234, 1.203, 1.168, 1.126, 1.088, 1.059, 1.035, 1.020 and 1.011.

questions.stem: Using only the survey note, which pair of statements is supported by the two sets of figures?

options.text: The gain rose and then fell while the per-individual rate fell throughout, so limits are tightening
The gain is the same every year, so this is a phase of steady exponential increase instead
options.misconception: reads a rising then falling gain as a constant one and calls it exponential

options.text: The per-individual rate is the same every year, so the gain must be constant as well
options.misconception: believes a constant per-capita rate forces a constant total gain

options.text: The gain is falling because fewer individuals are being born, rather than because of any limit
options.misconception: explains a falling total gain by fewer births and ignores the rising base it is on

questions.explanation: The two series move in opposite directions, and that is the signature of a population whose limits are closing. The gain climbs from 140 to 160 and then falls to 16, while the ratio of one year to the last falls the whole way from 1.28 to 1.011, so each individual is contributing less and less per year even though the population is still growing and still adding far more individuals each year than at the start. The tempting belief that a constant gain is exponential fails because the gain clearly changes. The belief that a constant per-individual rate forces a constant gain fails because a fixed fraction of a larger population is a larger number. The belief that fewer are being born fails because the number of births need not fall at all; what falls is births less deaths per head, and the base is rising.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Ecology: Testing Whether One Constant Rate Can Be Used
questions.learningObjective: test the constant-rate assumption from a table of differences and divergence times

stimulus.body: Comparison note (written for this course): Three pairs of related organisms are compared, and for each pair the number of differences in a chosen stretch of a molecule is counted together with the time since the two lineages are thought to have separated. Pair one shows 30 differences at 100 million years. Pair two shows 30 differences at 10 million years. Pair three shows 12 differences at 100 million years. Taking the ratio of differences to time gives 0.30, 3.00 and 0.12 differences per million years for the three pairs. The same method is used for all three, and the fossil record used to place the separation times is unchanged across the three.

questions.stem: Using only the comparison note, what do the three ratios show about the constant-rate idea behind this method?

options.text: The same number of differences covers times differing tenfold, so one rate cannot serve every pair
The three ratios are close enough that one rate can serve every pair without serious error
options.misconception: claims the rates agree when one is ten times another

options.text: The rates differ only because the method was applied with three different degrees of care
options.misconception: blames inconsistent technique rather than real variation in how fast changes accumulate

options.text: The rates cannot be compared, because the number of differences says nothing about the time taken
options.misconception: denies that a count of differences can be divided by a time at all

questions.explanation: The method assumes changes accumulate at a roughly constant rate, so that a count of differences can be converted into a time. The note shows the assumption failing: pairs one and two have the same count of differences over times that differ tenfold, so their rates differ by that same factor of ten, and pair three differs from pair one as well even though both are dated to the same interval. A clock with a single rate for all three would misdate at least two of them badly. This is why real dating uses more than one molecule, and why the molecule chosen has to be one accumulating at a defensible rate in that particular group. The tempting belief that the rates agree fails because the numbers differ tenfold. The belief about care in applying the method fails because the method was identical. The belief that a count says nothing about time fails because that is the whole premise of the method.
questions.hint: Divide differences by time for each pair, then compare the quotients.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Ecology: Why a Renewable Supply Can Defuse a Contest
questions.learningObjective: identify the role of scarcity in determining whether exclusion occurs

stimulus.body: Culture note (written for this course): Two species of microorganism are grown together in vessels whose growing medium is continuously renewed at a fixed rate. In the first vessel the nutrient arrives at 6 units an hour, in the second at 10, and in the third at 15. Grown alone, the first species needs 6 units an hour to hold its numbers steady and the second needs 4. In the first vessel only the first species is found after many hours. In the second both are found, the second of them at a low level. In the third both are found and the second of them is near the level it reaches alone.

questions.stem: Using only the culture note, what does the third vessel show about what exclusion actually requires?

options.text: The supply has to be scarce, since once it exceeds the combined need of ten there is no contest left
The supply has to be plentiful, since exclusion occurs when both species can be fully satisfied
options.misconception: reads plenty as the cause of exclusion when scarcity is what removes the loser

options.text: The species have to be kept apart, since the third vessel is the only one holding both of them
options.misconception: believes physical separation between the two is what exclusion requires

options.text: The species have to be kept together, since being separated in the first vessel spared neither one
options.misconception: believes the two must share a vessel and reads the first one as sparing neither

questions.explanation: Together the two species need 6 plus 4, which is 10 units an hour, and the third vessel supplies 15, so both can take what they need and neither is short enough to be pushed off the resource. The first vessel supplies only 6, which is not enough for the pair, so one of them cannot be supported at its needed rate and disappears. Exclusion is therefore a consequence of scarcity, not merely of two species sharing a resource, and the same result appears in a pond or a field wherever the supply is raised above what the competing individuals can take. The tempting belief that plentiful supply causes exclusion fails because nothing is being competed away. The belief about being kept apart fails because the two are together in all three vessels. The belief about being kept together fails because the third vessel is the one where both survive.
questions.hint: Add the two species' needs together and compare that total with each supply rate.

questions.topic: Ecology: Following a Change Through a Food Web
questions.learningObjective: predict the indirect effect of removing a link from a food web

stimulus.body: Web note (written for this course): A coastal food web is described with four named groups. The large algae feed the small fish, the small fish feed the large fish, and the small fish also feed the seabirds. The seabirds have no other food in this description. The large fish have no other food. The small fish eat nothing else and are eaten by nothing else. In one arm of the coast the seabirds are removed and everything else is left alone. questions.stem: Using only the web note, what single chain of effects accounts for both recorded changes?

Fewer seabirds let the algae rise, which then fed more small fish, so the fish were better fed
options.misconception: reverses the first link so the algae rise instead of being grazed down

options.text: Fewer seabirds let the large fish fall, which let the algae rise, which then starved the fish
options.misconception: invents a link from the seabirds to the large fish that the web does not contain

options.text: Fewer seabirds let the small fish rise, which starved the large fish, which then stopped eating algae
options.misconception: reverses the final link so the algae are spared rather than grazed down

The belief about the large fish failing fails because the seabirds are not shown as eating the large fish, so the large fish were untouched by the removal. The belief that the small fish starved the large fish out and that the algae were spared reverses the sign of the final step.

questions.topic: Ecology: Reading a Change After a Sudden Reduction
questions.learningObjective: distinguish a chance change in proportions from a change in the alleles themselves

stimulus.body: Genetics note (written for this course): At a site with a population of 2,000, the frequency of one allele is recorded as 0.40. A comparable site where 300 individuals survived is also sampled, and its allele frequency comes out at 0.37. Nothing about the allele itself was measured to have changed, and the two sites are the same species in the same habitat.

options.text: Chance decided which alleles the few survivors carried, and the smaller the group the larger the shift
The storm selected for the rarer allele, so the survivors were the ones that tolerated it best
options.misconception: turns a chance sample into a fitness advantage for the allele that fell in frequency

options.text: The allele frequency is set by the habitat, so the storm could only have had a small effect on it
options.misconception: ignores the two different results and makes the shift optional

options.text: The allele merged with its partner form, so the frequency fell because the pair was counted once
options.misconception: assumes two alleles at one locus fused into a single count

The belief that the habitat fixes the value fails because the two sites differ. The belief about merging forms fails because the two alleles at a locus are counted separately and do not fuse.

The recipients keep their own allele through the season and reproduce. Applying the movement to the two starting figures gives 0.82 in the first valley and 0.18 in the second. The belief that equal numbers cancel fails because the valleys had different frequencies to begin with, so equal numbers move unequal amounts of the allele in opposite directions. The belief that the allele is removed fails because a fraction of a population leaves a population, not the population.

They are analogous as forelimbs, because the animal that swims was not made to fly at all

The belief about wings fails because homology is about origin and the note gives none. questions.topic: Ecology: Telling a Mass Extinction From a Bad Year
questions.learningObjective: identify a mass extinction by its rate relative to the background

stimulus.body: Stratigraphy note (written for this course): A record is divided into eight equal intervals and the number of marine families lost is counted in each, giving 3, 2, 4, 2, 3, 48, 4 and 2. The seven intervals other than the sixth average 2.86 families, and the sixth interval lost 48 of the 100 families present at its start. The losses in that sixth interval were spread across the whole size range of the group, and no comparable interval appears anywhere else in the record, which runs for a further nine intervals after it.

questions.stem: Using only the stratigraphy note, on what basis is the sixth interval separated from the other seven?

options.text: Its rate of loss is about seventeen times the average of the others, and the losses are spread through the group
Its number of losses is higher than the others, and loss in any interval above the average is exceptional
options.misconception: treats any interval above zero as exceptional, which every quiet interval is

options.text: Its number of losses is higher, and an interval with any loss at all is a separate kind of event
options.misconception: calls any loss at all a separate kind of event and so deletes the background rate

options.text: Its losses are spread through the group, and a spread of losses alone makes an interval a mass extinction
options.misconception: thinks a spread of losses identifies a mass extinction with no rate change at all

questions.explanation: Losses of a few families happen all the time, and the note shows they are happening in seven of the eight intervals, so the count alone cannot separate an event. What separates the sixth is scale relative to that continuing background, and it is nearly seventeen times the average of the others, which is the rate comparison rather than the raw number. The spread through the size range is a second, independent sign, since an event that takes the small and the large alike is not one unlucky group failing. The tempting belief that being above average is enough fails because every one of the seven quiet intervals is above a rate of zero. The belief that any loss is exceptional fails because loss is the normal condition of these records. The belief that a spread alone is sufficient fails because a gradual squeeze on one part of a group would also spread losses across sizes without any rate change.
questions.hint: Compare the sixth interval with the average of the others, not with zero.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Ecology: Reading a Report of a Damaging Introduction
questions.learningObjective: identify the two features that let an introduction damage a community

stimulus.body: Field note (written for this course): A plant from another continent is planted in a garden border. In the note it is recorded that this plant is eaten by a caterpillar in its own range, and that of the seeds it produces most are carried away and germinate away from the parent. In the garden the same plant is planted in nine patches. Over three seasons the note records that it appeared in every patch by the end of the second season, that a local plant of the same growth form was found in only two patches, and that no caterpillar recorded in the note was ever seen on it. Two other introductions in the same county are recorded as present but not spreading.

questions.stem: Using only the field note, which pair of features best explains why this plant spread and the other two did not?

options.text: It disperses well, and it has escaped the checks that limited it where it came from
It disperses well, and it competes for a different resource from the plants already there
options.misconception: believes using a different resource is what lets a newcomer crowd out the residents

options.text: It competes for the same resource, and it is eaten by fewer animals than the plants already there
options.misconception: puts the two species on one resource and calls the absence of predators the whole account

options.text: It is eaten by fewer animals, and the two other introductions were dispersed by the wind instead
options.misconception: invents a dispersal route for the other two that the note never records

questions.explanation: The note gives both halves of the account. Dispersal is documented, because most of its seeds travel and germinate away from the parent, and that is why it reached every patch in two seasons. Its release from checks is documented too, because the caterpillar that eats it at home is not recorded on it in the garden, so the population that had been held down there is now free to increase. The two other introductions are recorded as neither spreading nor displacing anything, which is the ordinary case. The tempting belief that using a different resource explains it fails because a different resource is what would protect the resident plants, not what would let the newcomer crowd them out. The belief that the same resource is named fails because the note describes displacement of a plant of the same growth form, not sharing. The belief about the wind fails because the note says nothing about how the other two were dispersed and does describe this one.
questions.hint: Ask what the note records about how it got everywhere, and about what was keeping it small at home.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Ecology: Locating the Steepest Point of a Growth Curve
questions.learningObjective: read a growth table to find the size at which the absolute increase is greatest

stimulus.body: Growth note (written for this course): A population is followed under a model in which the yearly gain without any crowding is proportional to the number present, and the crowding term reduces that gain in proportion to how close the population is to the level the habitat can carry. The recorded population sizes are 200, 400, 500, 600, 800 and 1,000, and the recorded yearly gains at those sizes are 80, 120, 125, 120, 80 and 0. The habitat carries 1,000 individuals.

questions.stem: Using only the growth note, at which of the recorded sizes does the population add the most individuals in a year, and what does that tell you?

options.text: At 500, which is half the level the habitat carries, so the biggest total gain comes halfway up
At 1,000, which is the level the habitat carries and therefore where gains must be largest
options.misconception: believes the ceiling is where growth is fastest rather than where it stops

options.text: At 200, which is furthest from the limit and therefore the freest to grow without hindrance
options.misconception: believes being furthest from the limit gives the largest total gain

options.text: At 800, which is closest to the limit and therefore where gains must be largest
options.misconception: believes the steepest point sits just below the ceiling rather than half way up

questions.explanation: The table peaks in the middle, at 500 with a gain of 125, and that is exactly half the level the habitat carries. The reason is that two terms are in opposition: crowding reduces the gain as the population rises, and both terms are individually largest at opposite ends, so their product is greatest in between. That is also the point at which a population is easiest to overharvest, since removing individuals there lets the remainder regrow fastest, which is why the same number taken at 200 does far less good. The tempting belief that the gain is greatest at the limit fails because crowding has cancelled the whole gain there. The belief that it is greatest furthest from the limit fails because a small population has few individuals to add. The belief that the nearest to the limit gives most fails because the table shows the gain falling steeply between 500 and 1,000.
questions.hint: Find the largest entry in the gain column, then compare that size with the level the habitat carries.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Ecology: Reading a Pyramid of Energy
questions.learningObjective: read a pyramid of energy and account for the missing energy

stimulus.body: Pyramid note (written for this course): The energy held in one hectare of a grassland community is measured for four successive levels, starting with the plants. The figures are 10,000 units at the first level, 1,000 at the second, 100 at the third and 10 at the fourth. Taking the second figure as a fraction of the first gives one tenth, the third as a fraction of the second gives one tenth again, and the same for the fourth. The note also records that the measurements are of energy in living tissue at one moment, not of energy passing through in a year.

questions.stem: Using only the pyramid note, what fraction of the first level's energy is still present at the third level, and where did the rest go?

options.text: One hundredth, with most of the rest spent running each level and leaving as heat
One tenth, with most of the rest spent running each level and leaving as heat
options.misconception: reads one step along the pyramid as the whole two-step loss

options.text: One tenth, with most of the rest simply not eaten and left lying in the tissues of the first level
options.misconception: explains the loss as uneaten material rather than as running cost and heat

options.text: One hundredth, with most of the rest still present at the first level as tissue that was not consumed
options.misconception: pairs the right fraction with an account that ignores respiration entirely

questions.explanation: Two steps of one tenth each leave one hundredth, so from 10,000 units the third level holds 100, and the note's own quotients confirm the arithmetic. The missing 9,900 is not stored anywhere waiting to be used: each level spent its own share on breathing, moving and repair, and that spending leaves as heat which cannot be gathered back up by the next level. This is why a pyramid of energy is always steeply tapering while a pyramid of numbers need not be, since standing stock is a different measurement from the flow through it. The tempting belief that the fraction is one tenth fails because the note shows one tenth at each of two separate steps. The belief that the loss is uneaten tissue fails because material left uneaten is not energy that was spent; it is material that never entered the chain. The belief that heat is ignored fails because heat is the largest single destination.
questions.hint: Apply the one-tenth step twice, then think about what every level spends just to stay alive.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Ecology: Computing Density for Two Sites
questions.learningObjective: compute and compare population density from counts and areas

stimulus.body: Survey note (written for this course): Two sites of the same habitat are surveyed by the same method in the same week. At the first site 240 individuals of the species are counted across 600 square metres of habitat, and at the second site 300 are counted across 500 square metres. The counts are of the same species in both cases, and the effort per unit area is the same in both surveys. Dividing the count by the area gives 0.4 per square metre for the first site and 0.6 for the second.

questions.stem: Using only the survey note, which site holds the denser population and by how much?

options.text: The second, because 0.6 per square metre is one and a half times the 0.4 of the first
The first, because 240 individuals spread over 600 square metres is the denser count
options.misconception: prefers the larger total count without dividing by the area

options.text: Neither, because the second site has a larger total and the first has a larger area, so the two cancel
options.misconception: assumes a bigger count and a bigger area cancel without computing either

options.text: The second, because its larger total of 300 means the two sites hold the same number per hectare
options.misconception: asserts equal density from a difference in counts and areas

questions.explanation: Density is the count divided by the area, and doing that for the two sites gives 0.4 and 0.6 per square metre, so the second is the denser by a factor of one and a half even though the first site has more individuals altogether. That gap between a bigger total and a bigger density is the reason both measures are reported: the first site holds more animals and the second holds them more tightly packed. The tempting belief that 240 over 600 is the denser count fails because it is the smaller of the two quotients. The belief that the totals and areas cancel fails because they are not equal changes, and the quotients settle it. The belief about the same number per hectare fails because the two figures per square metre differ.
questions.hint: Divide each count by its own area before comparing anything.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Ecology: Reading a Pair of Monoculture and Mixed Cultures
questions.learningObjective: interpret a monoculture and mixed-culture comparison as evidence of competition

stimulus.body: Culture note (written for this course): Two species are grown in identical vessels. Grown alone, the first species reaches a density of 100 units and the second reaches 80. Grown together in one vessel, the first reaches 95 and the second reaches 5. The nutrient supply in every vessel is renewed at the same rate and the total is more than enough for either species alone. The second species is recorded as reaching 5, which is one twentieth of the 80 it reaches alone, while the first loses only 5 of its 100.

questions.stem: Using only the culture note, what does the size of the loss in each species show?

options.text: The loss falls almost entirely on the second, which is the pattern competition produces
The loss falls equally on both, because they are competing for one and the same nutrient
options.misconception: expects an even split of the loss between two species drawing on one resource

options.text: The loss falls almost entirely on the first, which is the pattern competition produces
options.misconception: puts the large loss on the wrong species and calls it the right pattern

options.text: Neither species lost anything real, because the vessel supplied more nutrient than either needed
options.misconception: ignores the difference between what was supplied and what was reached

questions.explanation: Whichever species loses the larger share of what it reaches alone is the one held down, and the note shows the first keeping 95 of its 100 while the second keeps 5 of its 80, so the second is the one being squeezed out. That asymmetry is the informative part, because a shortfall in supply would depress both and a change in conditions would depress both, whereas one species doing well while the other collapses points at the interaction between them. The fact that the total supply was ample rules out simple scarcity of the vessel's contents, which leaves the contest over who gets to it. The tempting belief that the loss is shared fails because the two losses are nothing like equal. The belief about the wrong species fails because it reverses which one is thriving. The belief that an ample supply removes the effect fails because plenty for one is not plenty for both when they draw on the same pool.
questions.hint: Express each final density as a fraction of what that species reached alone.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Ecology: Computing a Diversity Index From a Survey
questions.learningObjective: compute a diversity index for two communities and rank them

stimulus.body: Survey note (written for this course): Two ponds are surveyed, and each holds exactly 100 individuals of four species. In the first the four species are counted 25, 25, 25 and 25. In the second they are counted 88, 4, 4 and 4. Diversity is taken here as one minus the sum of the squares of the four proportions. For the first pond the four proportions are all 0.25 and their squares sum to 0.25, giving 0.75. For the second the proportions are 0.88, 0.04, 0.04 and 0.04, whose squares sum to 0.7792, giving 0.2208.

questions.stem: Using only the survey note, which pond is the more diverse, and on what does the answer rest?

options.text: The first, because both hold four species but its index is 0.75 against 0.2208
The second, because it has the same number of species as the first and more of them
options.misconception: calls a dominant-heavy pond more diverse because the species counts happen to tie

options.text: The second, because it supports a dominant species that the first pond does not have at all
options.misconception: treats the presence of a dominant species as a mark of diversity rather than of the reverse

options.text: They are equally diverse, because the count of four species is the same in each of them
options.misconception: equates equal richness with equal diversity and drops how the individuals are spread

questions.explanation: Both ponds hold four species, so richness ties them, and the index separates them because it also counts how the individuals are spread. The first pond's four equal proportions square to a quarter in total, giving 0.75, while the second pond's dominant species contributes most of the whole sum, giving 0.2208. The two answers differ by a factor of more than three on the same richness, which is the entire reason for using an index rather than a count. The tempting belief that the second is more diverse fails because it is nearly a one-species pond. The belief that a dominant species is itself a mark of diversity inverts the relationship. The belief that equal richness means equal diversity fails because it drops the distribution of individuals, which is the only thing the two ponds differ in.
questions.hint: Both ponds hold four species, so look at what the index adds to that count.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Ecology: Solving for the Prey Size Where Gains Meet Losses
questions.learningObjective: solve for the prey size at which growth and predation balance

stimulus.body: Model note (written for this course): A prey's yearly gain without predators is the number present multiplied by 0.5 and by the fraction of the habitat still unoccupied, on a habitat that carries 1,000. Loss to a predator is the number of prey multiplied by 0.0005 and multiplied by the number of predators, and the number of predators is held at 200 for the whole period by continual immigration. Gaining and losing balance when the two expressions are equal. Alone, with no predators present, the prey settles at 1,000. With predators held at 200, the two expressions are both equal to 80 when the prey stands at 800.

questions.stem: Using only the model note, at what prey size do gains and losses balance while 200 predators are held, and what has happened to that size?

options.text: At 800, which is two hundred below the 1,000 the prey reached without predators
At 1,000, which is the same size the prey reached without any predators present
options.misconception: believes a second loss term leaves the prey's own ceiling unchanged

options.text: At 200, which is the number of predators and so the point where the two cancel
options.misconception: takes the predator count as the prey's balance point instead of as a loss rate

options.text: At 1,200, which is above the level the prey reached without any predators present
options.misconception: supposes being eaten raises the prey's settled size above its uncrowded level

questions.explanation: Setting the two expressions equal and dividing by the number of prey gives that the fraction unoccupied equals 0.0005 times 200, which is 0.1, so the prey stands at nine tenths of 1,000, which is 800, and the note's own check of 80 against 80 confirms it. The comparison with 1,000 is the point of the item: adding a predator has not made the prey grow faster, it has lowered the size the prey settles at, because being eaten is a second loss sitting alongside running out of room. The tempting belief that the size is unchanged fails because the note's check of 80 against 80 holds at 800 and not at 1,000, where the prey has no further room to grow at all. The belief about the predator number fails because the predator count scales the losses, it does not set the prey size. The belief that the prey ends up above its uncrowded level fails because that would require the losses to be negative.
questions.hint: Set gain equal to loss, divide out the number of prey, and read off the unoccupied fraction.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Ecology: Design a Test for Density Dependence
questions.learningObjective: design a controlled test of whether a factor's effect depends on population density
questions.stem: A student claims that the spread of a disease through a colony is density-dependent, on the evidence that the disease was worse in one year than the last. Describe an experiment that would test the claim, and say why the student's evidence does not settle it.

answer.exemplar: Set up several identical enclosures and put deliberately different numbers of the same species into each, so the density is varied on purpose rather than allowed to vary by itself, then measure the same things in every enclosure: the total number of individuals, the number that became ill, and the number that died. Because density is the thing being manipulated, the comparison is between enclosures that differ in crowding and nothing else, and the enclosures should be kept at one temperature, one food supply and one cage size in terms of space per individual, with the assignment of numbers to positions made at random. A separate set of enclosures should be given a non-living stressor of comparable severity, such as a fixed temperature drop, at the same two densities, and that set is what shows what density-independent damage looks like. The student's evidence fails because density, time of year and the size of the colony all rise together in a colony that is growing, so a worse year is as easily explained by a colder month or a bigger population as by crowding. Only breaking the link between density and calendar time can separate the two.

questions.explanation: The design has to vary density by design, because a colony that grows on its own changes density and time at the same moment and the two cannot be told apart afterwards. A crowding-independent stressor is needed as the comparison that shows what non-density-dependent damage looks like.
questions.hint: Ask what else changes along with density in a colony that is simply getting bigger.
