questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Ecology: Design a Test for Competition for One Resource
questions.learningObjective: design a controlled test that two species compete for the same limiting resource
questions.stem: Two species are found together on a patch of ground, and a student claims they are competing for the same limiting resource. Describe an experiment that would test the claim, and say what result would count against it.

answer.exemplar: Grow the two species in three treatments that differ only in who is present: the first species alone, the second species alone, and the two together, all in containers of the same size with the same total supply of the resource and the same light and temperature. Measure both the size each species reaches and how much of the resource is left over at the end. If they are competing for the same limiting thing, each will do noticeably worse in the mixed container than in its own monoculture while the total they take remains close to the amount supplied, because one is taking what the other would have used. If instead each reaches the same size in the mixed container as alone, or if the mixed container still leaves resource unused at the end, the claim is not supported, since a genuine contest over a limiting supply cannot leave the supply plentiful. Measuring the leftover rather than only the two populations is the part that distinguishes competition from two species that simply share a place.

questions.explanation: The comparison that matters is between each species alone and the two together, and the leftover resource is what shows whether the supply was actually limiting. Equal performance in the mixture is the result that counts against the claim, because competition has to cost the competitors something.
questions.hint: Ask what you would have to compare against each species growing on its own.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Ecology: Design a Test for a Keystone Role
questions.learningObjective: design a controlled removal test for a keystone species
questions.stem: A rarely seen species is called keystone in a community. Describe an experiment that would test that claim, and explain why simply noting that the community still exists without it would not be enough.

answer.exemplar: Remove the species from a set of comparable plots and leave it in place in a matching set, with the plots matched beforehand for size, slope, soil and the abundance of the other species, and with the removal and the retention assigned at random. Before the removal, measure the same set of things in every plot: the cover or density of each other group present, the total of each, and one or two measures of what the community is doing, such as how much bare ground is left. Then repeat the measurements on a fixed schedule afterwards and compare the change in the removed plots with the change in the retained ones, because a community drifts on its own and only the difference between the two sets can be attributed to the removal. The claim that the community still exists is not enough, because a community can persist in a visibly degraded state with a few groups missing, and a keystone claim is about a change in the rest of the community that is large relative to how few individuals were removed. If the removed plots end up much like the retained ones, the species is common but not keystone here.

questions.explanation: The retained plots are the control that turns a before-and-after comparison into an attributable one, and the claim is about the change in the other species, not about whether the community technically still exists.
questions.hint: Ask what a comparison against the unremoved plots is for, and what would count as a change.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Ecology: Design a Test of Two Growth-Rate Constants
questions.learningObjective: design a controlled test comparing per-capita growth rates between two treatments
questions.stem: A claim is made that a population of a fungus grows faster on one medium than on another. Describe an experiment that would test the claim, and explain why comparing the two final sizes would not be enough.

answer.exemplar: Start the two treatments with the same small inoculum in identical flasks, hold everything except the medium the same, including volume, temperature, aeration and how often the flasks are shaken, and grow at least three flasks of each so the spread is visible. Measure the number of living units at a series of times rather than only at the end, and compare the treatments on the increase per unit per unit time, worked out between two consecutive counts in the rising part of the growth. Comparing only the final sizes fails because a slow culture that is given longer, or one that runs out of room later, can match a fast one, and because final size also reflects how much of the medium was left. The rising part is the only stretch where a per-capita rate is meaningful, since once a culture stops rising the rate reads as zero whatever the medium did, so a treatment measured only at that point has measured the supply of the medium rather than the fungus's use of it. One medium that supports a lower final total but a higher early rate is exactly the case this design would catch and an endpoint comparison would miss.

questions.explanation: A rate is a statement about a change per unit time per individual, so it has to be measured while the population is still rising, and it has to be measured per individual rather than at an endpoint. Replicates are what distinguish a real difference from one flask behaving oddly.
questions.hint: Ask which part of the growth curve can give a rate at all, and why an endpoint cannot.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Ecology: Design a Test That a Barrier Stops Movement
questions.learningObjective: design a controlled test of whether a barrier reduces movement between populations
questions.stem: Two groups of the same species are separated by a river. Describe an experiment that would test whether the barrier is holding them apart, and say what would count as evidence that it is not.

answer.exemplar: Look for the products of exchange rather than for the animals themselves, because a barrier that works is one that leaves no trace. Sample a marked, randomly chosen set of individuals on each side, score a trait that changes little within a lifetime, such as a coat pattern or a blood group, and then repeat the scoring on both sides in each of several later generations. Compare the two sides against a third group of the same species from a site with no barrier between it and either of them, which is what tells you whether any difference between the two sides is larger than the difference that accumulates between any two separated groups. If the barrier holds, the two sides drift further apart with every generation, so the differences grow, and the third group sits closer to both than they are to each other. If the barrier leaks, the two sides stay much closer to the third group than to each other would suggest, and the difference between them stops growing. Marking a few individuals and watching for them on the other side is a direct check, but it fails for anything that crosses at night, floods or is carried on the wind, so the scoring across generations is the more reliable of the two.

questions.explanation: A barrier is defined by what it stops, so the test looks for the absence of exchange, which shows up as a growing divergence between the two sides relative to an unbarriered comparison group. Watching for marked individuals alone would miss anything that crosses without being noticed.
questions.hint: Ask what you can measure after the animals have gone, and what a third group is needed for.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Ecology: Design a Test for Homology Against Analogy
questions.learningObjective: design a test that distinguishes a shared origin from a shared function
questions.stem: Two distant groups of animals are said to share a structure. Describe a test that would show whether the structure has a common origin or has arisen twice, and say why looking at what the structure does would not decide it.

answer.exemplar: Work out the origin of the structure, which means establishing the arrangement of its parts and where those parts sit relative to the rest of the animal, and then look at the developmental and historical record alongside that. Comparing several structures rather than one is what makes the test work: if the same set of parts in the same relative positions is present in both groups and in intermediate forms between them, the structure has one origin, and the differences in proportion are secondary reshaping. If the two structures are built from different parts in a different arrangement, and the record shows the parts appearing in the lineage only where the structure appears, then the structure arose twice, whatever the two do. Looking at function fails because the same job can be done by parts that arrived in completely different ways, and because a structure that has been remade for a new job stops resembling the one it came from in every respect except the job. That is precisely why proportion and exact resemblance are the least useful things to compare, and arrangement and developmental origin are the most useful.

questions.explanation: The test has to establish origin, which means the arrangement of parts and the developmental record, and function is the one thing that cannot distinguish a shared origin from two separate origins. Comparing several structures rather than one prevents a single match from being over-read.
questions.hint: Ask what would have to be recorded about the parts, and why the job the structure does cannot settle it.

questions.topic: Ecology: Checking a Year's Flows Against a Count
questions.learningObjective: compute a population change from flows and express it as a per-capita rate
questions.stem: A population of 500 is followed for a year. During the year 180 young are born and 30 individuals die, 12 immigrate from outside and 22 emigrate away, and an independent count at the end of the year gives 640. First work out the change the four flows imply, then work out that change as a fraction of the starting population.

options.text: A change of 140, which is 0.28 of the starting population and agrees with the count
A change of 150, which is 0.30 of the starting population and agrees with the count
options.misconception: leaves the emigrants out of the balance entirely

options.text: A change of 160, which is 0.32 of the starting population and disagrees with the count
options.misconception: adds migration going the wrong way and then ignores the disagreement

options.text: A change of 140, which is 0.20 of the ending population rather than of the starting one
options.misconception: divides by the ending population and so reports a different figure

questions.explanation: Births less deaths gives a gain of 150, immigration less emigration gives a loss of 10, and the net change is therefore 140, which turns 500 into 640 and so agrees with the independent count. As a fraction of the starting population that is 0.28, and that figure is the one to compare between two years or two places, because a change in absolute numbers is not comparable when the starting sizes differ. The tempting belief that the change is 150 fails because it omits the net loss of 10 to emigration. The belief that it is 160 fails because it counts the emigrants as arrivals, and the belief that it disagrees with the count fails because 500 plus 140 is exactly 640. The belief about dividing by the ending population fails because the rate is defined against the population at the start of the interval.
questions.hint: Work out the gain and the loss separately, then divide the net change by the number you began with.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Ecology: Comparing How Far Chance Moves a Frequency
questions.learningObjective: compute the sampling spread of an allele frequency at two population sizes
questions.stem: For a population of diploid individuals the spread of an allele frequency from one generation to the next is taken here as the square root of the quantity p times one minus p, divided by twice the number of individuals. Take p as 0.40. First work out that spread for a population of 50, then for a population of 5,000, and state the factor between the two.

options.text: About 0.049 and about 0.0049, so the larger population is ten times steadier
About 0.49 and about 0.0049, so the larger population is a hundred times steadier
options.misconception: drops a zero from the small-population figure and then compounds the error

options.text: About 0.049 both times, so the spread depends on p alone and not on the size
options.misconception: ignores the size term and claims the spread cannot change

options.text: About 0.24 and about 0.024, so the larger population is steadier but only by five times
options.misconception: adds the two halves of the expression instead of multiplying them

questions.explanation: For fifty individuals the quantity under the square root is 0.4 times 0.6 divided by 100, which is 0.0024, and its square root is about 0.049. For five thousand it is 0.24 divided by 10,000, which is 0.000024, and its square root is about 0.0049. The two differ by a factor of ten, and that is the whole content of the claim that chance matters more in small populations: the expected value of the frequency is unchanged in both, but the amount it wanders by is far larger when there are fewer gene copies to average over. The tempting belief that a hundred times is the factor fails because the denominator has a zero extra, not a factor of a hundred. The belief that the spread ignores size fails because the size is the term being varied. The belief about adding the halves fails because the expression multiplies them.
questions.hint: Work the denominator out first for each size, then take the square root of the whole thing.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Ecology: Following a Difference Between Two Populations
questions.learningObjective: compute how movement changes a difference and how long the change takes
questions.stem: An allele is at 0.90 in one population and 0.10 in a neighbouring one. In each generation a tenth of each population is made up of individuals that arrived from the other, and the rest keep their own allele. First work out the difference between the two frequencies after one generation, then work out roughly how many generations that generation must be repeated for the original difference to be halved.

options.text: 0.64, and about seven generations, since each generation keeps nine tenths of the gap
0.90, and about one generation, since the two populations have been made identical at once
options.misconception: believes one generation of movement mixes the two populations completely

options.text: 0.80, and about ten generations, since the original difference is unchanged by a single step
options.misconception: claims the difference survives a generation untouched and then times the halving wrongly

options.text: 0.64, and about one generation, since the smaller figure has already reached the larger one
options.misconception: uses the right gap and then claims it closed in a single generation

questions.explanation: With a tenth moving each way, the first population becomes nine tenths of 0.90 plus a tenth of 0.10, which is 0.82, and the second becomes 0.18, so the difference is 0.64 where it started at 0.80. Each generation keeps nine tenths of whatever difference is there, so the difference falls geometrically, and getting it down to 0.40 takes the number of doublings of a halving that 0.9 raised to takes, which is between six and seven generations. That is the sense in which movement opposes divergence: it does not reverse it in a single step, it subtracts a fixed fraction of the difference on every generation. The tempting belief that the two are identical at once fails because only a tenth moved. The belief that the difference is unchanged fails because 0.64 is not 0.80. The belief that the first generation halves it fails because nine tenths of 0.80 is 0.72, not 0.40.
questions.hint: Find the fraction of the difference that survives one generation, then work out how many halvings that buys.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Ecology: Working Out an Index for Two Communities
questions.learningObjective: compute a diversity index for two communities and rank them
questions.stem: Two ponds are each found to hold 100 individuals. In the first the individuals are divided 50, 30 and 20 between three species, and in the second 70, 20 and 10. Diversity is taken here as one minus the sum of the squares of the proportions in each pond. First work out the value for each pond, then state which pond is more diverse and why the species counts do not settle the question.

options.text: 0.62 against 0.46, so the first is more diverse although both ponds hold three species
0.38 against 0.54, so the second is more diverse although both ponds hold three species
options.misconception: reports the sums rather than one minus the sum, and names the wrong pond

options.text: 0.62 against 0.46, so the two ponds are equally diverse because both hold three species
options.misconception: gets both figures right and then declares the index irrelevant

options.text: 0.25 against 0.09, so the first is more diverse because its three proportions are nearest equal
options.misconception: sums the proportions instead of their squares and reads the wrong result

questions.explanation: For the first pond the squared proportions are 0.25, 0.09 and 0.04, which sum to 0.38, so the index is 0.62. For the second they are 0.49, 0.04 and 0.01, which sum to 0.54, so the index is 0.46. Both ponds hold three species, so the species count ties them and the index is what separates them, and it separates them because the first spreads its individuals more evenly. The tempting belief that the sums are the index fails because the definition is one minus the sum, which is why a larger sum of squares means a smaller diversity. The belief that the ponds tie fails because the index is exactly the thing added to the count for this reason. The belief about summing the proportions fails because they are squared first, and 0.25, 0.09 and 0.04 are the squares rather than the proportions.
questions.hint: Square each proportion, add the squares, and then take one minus that sum.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Ecology: Working Out Two Divergence Rates
questions.learningObjective: compute two implied rates and state the consequence of applying one of them to both
questions.stem: A dating method counts differences in a chosen stretch of a molecule and divides by a rate to get a time. For one pair of lineages the count is 30 differences and their separation is put at 100 million years, and for another pair the count is also 30 differences with a separation put at 10 million years. First work out the rate each pair implies, then state what would happen if the slower of the two were used for both.

options.text: 0.30 and 3.00 per million years, so the second pair would be dated ten times too far back
3.00 and 0.30 per million years, so the first pair would be dated ten times too near the present
options.misconception: reports the two rates the wrong way round and then dates the wrong pair

options.text: 0.30 and 0.03 per million years, so the second pair would be dated ten times too near the present
options.misconception: loses a zero in the second rate and then inverts the direction of the error

options.text: 0.30 and 3.00 per million years, so a single rate would be defensible because the counts agree
options.misconception: gets both rates right and then draws the opposite conclusion from them

questions.explanation: Thirty differences over a hundred million years is three tenths of a difference per million years, and thirty over ten million years is three, so the two pairs imply rates differing by a factor of ten. Using the slower rate for the second pair would put its thirty differences at a hundred million years, when the note's own separation for it is ten million years, so the date would be ten times too old. That is the concrete cost of the constant-rate assumption failing, and it is why a single molecule cannot be trusted across widely separated groups. The tempting belief that the rates are the other way round fails because the larger count per unit time belongs to the pair with the shorter separation. The belief that the second rate is 0.03 fails because 30 over 10 is 3. The belief that equal counts make one rate defensible fails because the counts are equal and the times are not, which is precisely the problem.
questions.hint: Divide each count by its own time, then ask what the slower rate would do to the pair that needs the faster one.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Ecology: Why the Term Climax Is Now Used Carefully
questions.learningObjective: explain why succession is not expected to reach a fixed endpoint
questions.stem: Succession is still taught as a sequence that ends in a final community. Explain why that word is now used more carefully than it once was, and what the alternative is to talk about.

answer.exemplar: The word promises a settled endpoint. It assumes that a community passes through a series of stages and then arrives at a composition that holds steady while the site stays as it is, and that is a strong claim, because it makes a prediction about the future rather than describing the past. Long records of the same sites show the prediction failing: species keep arriving and going, the composition keeps shifting, and a stretch that looks settled is a long plateau rather than an arrival. Climax species are not absent, they persist, and the best a site may do is approach a composition close to what was first described for it, which is why the term is often hedged with a word like potential. The alternative is to describe what the site is doing at a given time and to expect it to be replaced or rearranged, and to explain the pattern by the processes operating on it: which organisms build the soil, which ones fix nitrogen, which tolerate the conditions, and how those roles are filled by different species in different places. The tempting belief that the staging is what has failed fails because the order in which species arrive is broadly repeatable and is not in dispute. The belief that a settled site is one without disturbance fails because disturbance has always been part of the old account, and a site left alone still changes. The belief that the term is simply outdated and should be dropped fails because the idea of a community that is hard to displace is a real one and remains worth naming.

questions.explanation: The explanation has to identify the promise the term makes about the future and then show that the record does not keep it, because that is the whole reason the hedging was introduced.
questions.hint: Ask what the word asserts will happen next, and whether the record shows that happening.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Ecology: Why Movement Slows Divergence
questions.learningObjective: explain how movement between populations holds their frequencies together
questions.stem: Two neighbouring populations of the same species are kept apart in all the ways that matter, yet over generations they become more similar rather than less. Explain how movement of individuals accounts for that, using the arithmetic.

answer.exemplar: Movement of individuals is the one influence that repeatedly puts alleles back into a population from outside, and every time it does, the frequency in the receiving population moves a little way towards the frequency in the sending one. The arithmetic makes the size of the effect plain. If one valley is at 0.90 and the next at 0.10, a gap of 0.80, and a tenth of each population is replaced by arrivals from the other in each generation, the first becomes nine tenths of 0.90 plus a tenth of 0.10, which is 0.82, and the second becomes 0.18, so the gap falls to 0.64. Each generation therefore keeps nine tenths of whatever gap is there, and taking 0.9 to a power shows that halving the gap takes about seven generations. Nothing about the barriers between the valleys changes that: a river, a ridge or a field boundary is a wall to the water or the animal, not to a pollen grain or a wandering individual, and even a partial barrier leaks enough to hold the frequencies close. This is why the forces that separate populations, which are selection and the random loss of alleles, are resisted by the one influence that mixes them, and why a population that is well isolated is the one in which those forces act most freely. The tempting belief that movement makes the two identical at once fails because only the fraction that moves is exchanged in any one generation. The belief that equal numbers moving cancel fails because the two sides started at different frequencies, so equal numbers move different amounts of the allele.

questions.explanation: The explanation has to combine the mechanism with the arithmetic, because the size of the opposing effect is what shows why movement wins over many generations rather than in one step.
questions.hint: Ask what a fixed fraction of the difference does to the gap on each successive generation.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Ecology: Why a Branch Point Is an Inference
questions.learningObjective: explain what a node on a tree of relationships represents and what it is not
questions.stem: A tree of relationships is drawn for six living organisms with a branch point at the base and four more above it. Explain what each branch point stands for, and why no dead organism needs to be drawn at any of them.

answer.exemplar: A branch point on a tree of relationships marks the most recent ancestor of everything branching above it, so the lowest one is the ancestor of all six and each of the four above it is the ancestor of a smaller group. The point is that no body is recovered there. A tree is inferred from the pattern of similarities and differences among the living forms, and the ancestor at any branch point is the simplest organism consistent with that pattern, so the branch point is a conclusion about descent rather than a find. That is also why a tree can be drawn for a group in which no fossils at all exist, and why the age of a branch point comes from a separate source such as a dated rock layer or a calibrated molecule, both of which can be wrong without the shape of the tree changing. It also explains why the shape and the dates are two separate claims, so a disagreement about one is not automatically a disagreement about the other. The tempting belief that a branch point is a fossil fails because fossils are placed on a tree as a recovered form, and they are not the same thing as a node. The belief that the oldest point is at the top fails because the ordering of time on the tree is what puts the base at the base. The belief that the node marks a split into two species fails because whether a branch point represents a species split is decided by separate evidence about whether the two can reproduce together.

questions.explanation: The explanation has to separate the shape of the tree from the branch points and from the dates, because those are three different claims and conflating them is the usual error.
questions.hint: Ask what evidence the node is built from, and what would be drawn if a body had been found there.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Ecology: A Claim the Evidence Cannot Separate From Its Alternative
questions.learningObjective: explain why an absent trait cannot be read as evidence of a double origin
questions.stem: A structure is present in two groups of animals that are not close relatives, and a student concludes it must have arisen twice. Explain why the evidence the student has cannot tell the two origins apart from the alternative, and what would be needed to decide.

answer.exemplar: The structure's presence in two separate branches is equally consistent with two stories. Either it arose once in a common ancestor and was retained in both branches and lost everywhere else, or it arose twice, once in each branch. The evidence the student is using cannot separate these, and the reason is structural rather than a matter of effort: a tree shows where the branches are, and the tips show what each branch has, but a trait missing from a branch carries two possible readings, presence from the ancestor with a later loss, or absence because it was never gained there. The absence is not itself evidence for the second origin, because a trait can be lost for reasons that have nothing to do with where it came from. Two things would move the question forward. The first is the distribution among the intervening forms, because a structure present in the older relatives of one branch and absent only from the younger ones points to a loss on that branch, whereas a structure absent from all the relatives of that branch and present only in the modern tip points to a separate origin. The second is the arrangement of the parts, because a structure built from the same parts in the same relative positions is more easily explained by one origin, while one built from different parts is more easily explained by two. The tempting belief that two distant groups must have evolved it twice fails because distance is not evidence about the number of origins. The belief that the ancestor had it because both groups have it now fails because that assumes the answer, since loss is exactly the alternative that cannot be excluded. The belief that the simpler explanation settles it fails because deciding which is simpler requires the two lines of evidence that have just been described, not the pattern of presence and absence alone.

questions.explanation: The explanation has to show that a missing trait carries two readings and cannot be read as evidence for a double origin on its own, then name the two kinds of evidence that would decide it.
questions.hint: Ask what a trait that is absent from a branch might mean, and why that question cannot be answered from the tree alone.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Ecology: Ordering the Stages of Isolation Leading to Speciation
questions.learningObjective: order the stages by which geographic isolation can produce a new species
questions.stem: Put these four events in the order in which they must occur for a geographic barrier to produce a new species.

options.text: A change in the landscape separates the previously connected group into two
With no exchange between them, mutation and selection push the two groups apart
Differences accumulate until the two can no longer reproduce successfully together
The barrier is breached, and their offspring show how far apart the two have become

questions.explanation: The barrier has to come first because the whole mechanism depends on the exchange of individuals stopping, and it is the stopping of that exchange which lets the two groups change independently under mutation, chance loss and whatever selection acts on them. Reproductive isolation has to build up while they are apart, because until it has, lifting the barrier would simply remix the two. The final test comes when they meet again, and it is a real test rather than a formality because until then the two are only diverged populations, not separate species. The tempting wrong order that puts the breach first fails because a barrier that is not there cannot have caused anything. The wrong order that puts the offspring test before isolation has built fails because offspring produced too early would be fertile and would blend the groups again.
questions.hint: Start with whatever stops the exchange, and put the test of separation after the differences have built up.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Ecology: Ordering the Steps of Primary Succession
questions.learningObjective: order the stages by which a community establishes itself on bare ground
questions.stem: Put these four events in the order in which they occur on a surface where no soil has ever been present.

options.text: Weathering breaks the surface and a thin layer of raw material begins to form
Organisms that can manage without soil arrive, and their remains start to build one
Plants that need a developed soil root in the accumulating material and spread
A closed community develops, and further change continues within it over time

questions.explanation: The sequence begins before any organism is involved, because bare rock has to be broken down before there is anything for the first colonisers to work on. Those colonisers are the ones that can cope with no soil, and their contribution is the first organic material, which is what turns raw rock into something that can hold water. Only once there is a soil of that kind can the plants that need a developed rooting medium arrive, and they in turn change the light and moisture on the surface, which is what allows the later arrivals. The last step is a community that is broadly closed, and the ordering is what matters: the term describes the whole progression on ground where soil was destroyed, and it is slower than the corresponding progression where soil survives. The tempting wrong order that puts the plants before the first organisms fails because the plants are the ones that needed the soil the earlier ones made. The wrong order that puts the closed community before the spread of plants fails because the closed community is built out of the plants that come earlier.
questions.hint: Start with what has to happen to the rock before anything can grow on it at all.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Ecology: Ordering the Events of a Selective Sweep
questions.learningObjective: order the events by which one allele spreads through a population and carries linked variants
questions.stem: Put these four events in the order in which they occur when one strongly favoured allele rises through a population that has been varying.

options.text: One of the existing variants confers a clear advantage in the conditions of the time
Carriers of that variant leave more descendants, so its frequency climbs quickly
Variants linked to it rise with it, whether or not they confer an advantage of their own
The variants it dragged along fall as it approaches fixation, leaving the region short of variation

questions.explanation: A sweep needs a variant that is genuinely favoured under the conditions at the time, because a variant that is merely common has nothing to sweep. Once favoured, its carriers reproduce more, and the frequency climbs steeply rather than drifting, which is the part that distinguishes it from chance. Because the genome is inherited in blocks rather than variant by variant, whatever happens to be attached to the favoured allele is carried along with it, including variants that are neutral or even slightly harmful, and that hitchhiking is what a linked population is dragged through. The final step is the consequence everybody finds surprising: as the favoured allele approaches fixation there is nothing left for the linked variants to hitchhike on, so the population that has been swept over is left with less variation around it than before, which is the trace the event leaves behind. The tempting wrong order that puts the hitchhiking before the rise fails because nothing is carried until there is something worth carrying. The wrong order that puts the loss of variation first fails because the region only thins as the sweep runs out.
questions.hint: Start with why one variant rises, then follow what is attached to it, then the end state.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Ecology: Ordering the Passages of a Nutrient in a Community
questions.learningObjective: order the routes by which a nutrient passes through an ecosystem and its reservoir
questions.stem: Put these four events in the order in which a nutrient moves through an ecosystem and returns to its reservoir.

options.text: The nutrient is taken out of the reservoir by the primary producers of the community
It passes into the animals that eat the producers, part of it travelling inside them
It leaves the living organisms as waste and as dead material, reaching the decomposers
Decomposers release it back into the reservoir, from where the producers can take it again

questions.explanation: The cycle has to start at the reservoir, because that is the store the nutrient waits in and the only place it is drawn from. Producers take it out of that store and into living tissue, which is the one point in the cycle where the nutrient is out of the reservoir and doing something, and everything after that is the same material passing through consumers. It leaves the living organisms as waste and as death rather than staying locked in them, and the decomposers are what return it, so the cycle is a loop rather than a line. Keeping the ordering straight matters because it shows that a reservoir is doing the work in the cycle: carbon in the air and nitrogen in the air are the buffers that let a system keep going while producers and decomposers are out of step. The tempting wrong order that puts the decomposers before the animals fails because the decomposers act on what the organisms leave, not on the animals while they live. The wrong order that puts the return to the reservoir last but before the decomposers fails because it is the decomposers that make the return possible.
questions.hint: Start with the store, and remember that the same material passes through every living group on the way round.
